spans.heading: History
spans.text: By 1913, 2,300,000 were insured under the unemployment benefit programme.

spans.heading: History
spans.text: The dole system provided 39 weeks of unemployment benefits to over 11,000,000 workers—practically the entire civilian working population except domestic service, farmworkers, railway men, and civil servants.

spans.heading: Unemployment benefits effect on unemployment
spans.text: Conservative economist Robert Barro found that benefits raised the unemployment rate 2%.

spans.heading: Unemployment benefits effect on unemployment
spans.text: Disagreeing with Barro's study were Berkeley economist Jesse Rothstein, who found the "vast majority" of unemployment was due to "demand shocks" not "[unemployment insurance]-induced supply reductions."

spans.heading: Unemployment benefits effect on unemployment
spans.text: A study by Rothstein of extensions of unemployment insurance to 99 weeks during the Great Recession to test the hypothesis that unemployment insurance discourages people from seeking jobs found the overall effect of UI on unemployment was to raise it by no more than one-tenth of 1%.

spans.heading: Unemployment benefits effect on unemployment
spans.text: A November 2011 report by the Congressional Budget Office found that even if unemployment benefits convince some unemployed to ignore job openings, these openings were quickly filled by new entrants into the labour market.

spans.heading: Unemployment benefits effect on unemployment
spans.text: A survey of studies on unemployment insurance's effect on employment by the Political Economy Research Institute found that unemployed who collected benefits did not find themselves out of work longer than those who did not have unemployment benefits; and that unemployed workers did not search for work more or reduce their wage expectations once their benefits ran out.

spans.heading: Unemployment benefits effect on unemployment
spans.text: Arash Nekoei and Andrea Weber present empirical evidence from Austria that extending unemployment benefit duration raises wages by improving reemployment firm quality.

spans.heading: Unemployment benefits effect on unemployment
spans.text: Similarly, Tatsiramos studied data from European countries and found that although unemployment insurance does increase unemployment duration, the duration of subsequent employment tends to be longer (suggesting better match quality).

spans.heading: Unemployment benefits effect on unemployment
spans.text: It has also been shown that allowing self-employed individuals to access unemployment insurance might lead to a boost in self-employment activity.

spans.heading: Funding
spans.text: According to The Council of State Governments, by 18 March 2011, 32 states plus the Virgin Islands had borrowed nearly $45.7 billion.

spans.heading: Funding
spans.text: The Labour Department estimates by the fourth quarter of 2013, as many as 40 states may need to borrow more than $90 billion to fund their unemployment programs and it will take a decade or more to pay off the debt.

spans.heading: Systems by country
spans.text: Countries with higher unemployment benefits do not have higher rates of unemployment.

spans.heading: Canada
spans.text: The ratio of beneficiaries to unemployed, after having stood at around 40% for many years, rose somewhat during the 2009 recession but then fell back again to the low 40s.

spans.heading: Canada
spans.text: Total EI spending was $19.677 billion for 2011–2012 (figures in Canadian dollars).

spans.heading: Canada
spans.text: Premiums were reduced much less than falling expenditures – producing, from 1994 onwards, EI surpluses of several billion dollars per year, which were added to general government revenue.

spans.heading: Canada
spans.text: The cumulative EI surplus stood at $57 billion at 31 March 2008, nearly four times the amount needed to cover the extra costs paid during a recession.

spans.heading: France
spans.text: In 2011, claimants received the allowance for an average 291 days.

spans.heading: Iceland
spans.text: In the most recent financial quarter, 85.8% of the Icelandic working-age population were employed, with only 2.8% of the population unemployed.

spans.heading: Iceland
spans.text: Only 11.9% of the working population is dependent on temporary employment.

spans.heading: Israel
spans.text: The unemployment rate in Israel in 2009 had been 9.5% and has since dropped to around 4% in 2018.

spans.heading: Mexico
spans.text: However, this does not cover the majority of workers, as 58% of the labour force is in the informal sector.

spans.heading: United States
spans.text: Receipt varies substantially by state; nationally, roughly one in four unemployed people received unemployment insurance in 2025.
